title: Assessing the potential of runs of homozygosity to infer stock status of commercial bivalves under ongoing anthropogenic disturbances
content:
Abstract
Assessing population status through time is critical for management, conservation, and domestication of species under frequent anthropogenic disturbances, in which inbreeding degree and selection signature are two key genetic components to consider. Bivalves have great ecological and economic values but are highly susceptible to anthropogenic activities. Thus, it is essential to constantly evaluate their population status. While runs of homozygosity (ROH) has the potential to reveal true inbreeding level and uncover distinct selection footprints, whether and how it can be applied to infer stock status of bivalves remains nearly unexplored. Here, we conduct genome-wide ROH scanning for four representative natural stocks of a commercially important marine bivalve, Zhikong scallop Chlamys farreri, which has gone through drastic demographic changes driven by overfishing and aquaculture over the past 70 years in China. Our study suggests that rule-based methods are more sensitive to parameter settings than model-based methods. Rule-based methods with appropriate parameter settings and RZooRoH perform equally well. Given that determining parameter settings for rule-based methods is computationally demanding and time consuming, RZooRoH appears to be a more suitable and efficient approach at least for preliminary evaluations in scallop and other similar species. In cases where rule-based methods are needed, the influence of parameter settings should be thoroughly investigated. The weak correlation between FROH and other inbreeding measures implies that FROH may not be able to accurately reflect inbreeding in natural scallop stocks. As whether FROH correlates well with other genetic metrics for inbreeding and diversity varies across study systems, FROH should be assessed case by case before it can be used to estimate inbreeding in aquatic invertebrates. A variety of selection signatures are revealed, among which ROH deserts could be ascribed to either selection against recessive deleterious alleles or selection for overdominant alleles whereas ROH islands suggest positive selection. Although ROH deserts and islands arise from distinct types of selection, they are associated with a set of shared biological processes, including nervous system development, DNA repair, and transcription regulation. Our findings have broad implications for management, conservation, and domestication for not only scallop but also other similar aquatic invertebrates.
